titre: Caremark (1996): The Duty of Oversight Is Born in an Approval Ruling
accroche: On September 25, 1996, a Delaware judge lays down the duty to see that an information system exists, then finds that Caremark had one and approves the settlement.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 25, 1996, Chancellor Allen of the Delaware Court of Chancery (United States) convicts no one. He must say whether a settlement proposed in a shareholder suit is fair and reasonable. The suit targets the directors of Caremark International, a health care services company: they allegedly breached their duty of care by letting employees violate federal and state laws applicable to health care providers. The losses are heavy. After four years of investigation by the U.S. Department of Health, Caremark is indicted in 1994 on several felony counts, pleads guilty to mail fraud, and the sums it must pay reach about $250 million.

## What the board had already put in place

The dispute turns on contracts with physicians. An American law prohibits a provider from paying anyone to bring in patients covered by Medicare or Medicaid. Caremark's contracts, which paid physicians for consulting or patient follow-up, were not prohibited in themselves, but the opinion notes that they could obviously open the door to illegal kickbacks. It lists what the company had done: an internal guide to contractual relationships, in use since 1989 at its predecessor and reviewed each year by lawyers; since September 1992, approval of every contract with a physician by a regional officer; an ethics manual approved on July 27, 1993, which prohibits payments in exchange for patient referrals and opens a confidential hotline for reporting illegal acts.

## A duty stated, a very high threshold

Allen refuses to read broadly a 1963 Delaware Supreme Court decision, *Graham v. Allis-Chalmers*, according to which a board, without grounds for suspecting deception, need not doubt the honesty of its employees. A board, he writes, cannot claim to be informed without having made sure that information channels exist in the company. He also notes that the federal sentencing guidelines for organizations (chapter 8 of the November 1994 manual) offer powerful incentives to set up compliance programs.

But he sets the threshold of liability very high. Only a sustained or systematic failure of oversight, for example the utter failure to attempt to put in place a reasonable system, would establish the lack of good faith required. This theory is, he says, possibly the most difficult theory in corporation law upon which a plaintiff might hope to win.

## The shift

Applied to the record, the rule turns to the directors' advantage. The chancellor finds almost no evidence of a sustained failure: the company's information systems seem to him a good-faith attempt to be informed, and he judges the claims extremely weak. The settlement, whose financial component had been withdrawn during negotiation, contains only commitments: not to pay anyone in exchange for patient referrals, and to have the board review regulatory changes twice a year. Allen sees in it a very modest benefit, approves it, and awards the plaintiffs' attorneys $816,000 in fees and $53,000 in expenses, out of $1,025,000 requested.

The sentence that lawyers cite to ground the duty of oversight was thus born in a case where that duty was not found to have been violated, and where the decisive argument was that the board did have a system. The duty thus laid down is not to know everything: it is to make sure that information flows upward. What the text leaves open remains: how far must a system function before one can say that it exists?

citation.texte: a director's obligation includes a duty to attempt in good faith to assure that a corporate information and reporting system, which the board concludes is adequate, exists
citation.auteur: Chancellor Allen, Delaware Court of Chancery
citation.source: In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation, 698 A.2d 959 (Del. Ch. 1996)

carte.punch: Directors' duty of oversight is born in a ruling that approves a settlement.
carte.idee: On September 25, 1996, Chancellor Allen (Delaware) writes that a director must attempt in good faith to make sure an information system exists. Yet he judges the claims against Caremark's directors extremely weak and approves the settlement.
carte.source_courte: In re Caremark, Del. Ch., September 25, 1996

quiz.question: Why do Caremark's directors escape all liability even though the opinion lays down a duty of oversight?
choix: The duty of oversight did not apply to crimes committed by a company's employees
The directors had reimbursed the sums paid to the government out of their own pockets, which extinguished the claims
Nothing established a sustained failure: a guide, an ethics manual, and a committee existed and the board was informed
The law on payments to physicians was too obscure for its violation to be held against the board
quiz.explication: The chancellor does not say that oversight is beside the point, nor that the directors paid, nor that the law was too obscure: he finds that nothing shows a sustained or systematic failure, since the company had a guide, an ethics manual, and information channels. A huge loss born of an offense is not enough to violate the duty.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which earlier Delaware Supreme Court decision does Chancellor Allen refuse to read broadly in Caremark?
choix: Smith v. Van Gorkom (1985)
Graham v. Allis-Chalmers (1963)
Aronson v. Lewis (1984)
Unocal Corp. v. Mesa Petroleum (1985)
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry cites specifically Graham v. Allis-Chalmers, from 1963, according to which a board without grounds for suspecting deception need not doubt the honesty of its employees; Allen refuses a broad reading of it rather than setting it aside.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the ethics manual approved by Caremark on July 27, 1993 put in place?
choix: An obligation to send each contract to the Department of Health before signing
A prohibition on payments in exchange for patient referrals, with a confidential hotline to report them
The elimination of all consulting contracts with outside physicians
A mandatory annual audit by an independent firm
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that this manual, approved on July 27, 1993, prohibits payments in exchange for patient referrals and opens a confidential hotline for reporting illegal acts, without eliminating consulting contracts or creating any obligation toward the Department or an outside auditor.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the federal sentencing guidelines for organizations (chapter 8, November 1994) stress, according to the opinion?
choix: They forbid health care services companies from contracting with physicians
They impose a minimum sentence of $250 million on convicted companies
They require every board of directors to appoint a regional officer
They offer powerful incentives to set up compliance programs
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the opinion notes that these guidelines offer powerful incentives to set up compliance programs; it attributes to them neither a ban on medical contracts, nor a mandatory minimum sentence, nor an obligation to appoint a regional officer.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the settlement ultimately approved by Allen made up, after the financial component was withdrawn during negotiation?
choix: It provides for a fine paid by the directors personally
It requires the resignation of half of the board of directors
It contains only commitments, including a twice-yearly review of regulatory changes by the board
It transfers responsibility for oversight to an outside federal body
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that the settlement, once the financial component was withdrawn, contains only commitments: not to pay anyone in exchange for patient referrals, and to have the board review regulatory changes twice a year.
